units.text: This is Professor Chapman, and you are aboard the Grateful Dead at Hampton Coliseum in Hampton, Virginia, on May the first, 1981. That first set is the reason we came, with an unhurried Friend of the Devil, real heat from Garcia in Althea, and a Let It Grow into Deal that I would place among the finest of the era. Opinion divides on the second set, and I'll admit that freely, since some listeners find it pedestrian once the drummers take over. But the opening Feel Like a Stranger into Franklin's Tower simply refuses to stop, and later, when He's Gone dissolves into The Other One, the whole room tilts toward the psychedelic. I would urge you not to wander off during that particular passage.

units.text: That was the first set from the Grateful Dead at the Richmond Coliseum in Richmond, Virginia, November first, nineteen eighty-five, and you're listening to One More from the Archive. We heard that rare opening pair, a cowboy double of Me And My Uncle and Big River, a lively Brown Eyed Women, and then Jack Straw carrying us home into Don't Ease Me In. Now we come to one of the strangest second sets of the whole decade. After Samson And Delilah, the band settles into five slow, searching songs in a row: High Time, He's Gone, Spoonful, Comes A Time, and Lost Sailor. It feels less like a rock show and more like the mellowest night of the Jerry Garcia Band, as though the entire Coliseum had drifted out past the orbit of Neptune for the better part of an hour. Then a long Drums separates Lost Sailor from Saint Of Circumstance, the only time that pairing was ever split by another piece of music. Stay with me for a Dylan rarity in She Belongs To Me, and a raucous Gloria to bring the set home.

units.text: You're listening to One More from the Archive, and that was the first set from the Grateful Dead at Freedom Hall in Louisville, Kentucky, on June the eighteenth, nineteen seventy-four. I hope you caught Keith Godchaux taking the first solo in Eyes Of The World, then adding that triumphant harmony to the seven-eight outro, before the band drifted down into a lovely China Doll, and then closed the set with a positively ferocious ending. The second set is where this evening earns its reputation. After a bouncy, funky Loose Lucy, a speedy El Paso, and a Row Jimmy with pristine slide work, comes a sequence that runs nearly an hour. It moves from Weather Report Suite into Let It Grow, and then into The Other One, where Phil Lesh unveils his new quad bass. Out of that rises an instrumental jam on It's A Sin, the old Eddy Arnold country hit, which the band played on this night and never again, before the music opens into Stella Blue. If the cosmos keeps a waiting room, I imagine it sounds like those few minutes. Big River, Tennessee Jed and Sugar Magnolia bring the set home, and I'd suggest you not wander off when it ends. Once more, this is the Grateful Dead at Freedom Hall in Louisville.
